Mikel Arteta is still king in the Premier League, with rivals struggling with intensity

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

‘Intensity’ is the buzzword of the moment, capturing a vibe that is just so Premier League.

For armchair tacticians - in particular for those pundits who lack the capacity for tactical analysis but know they ought to have this sort of thing down - ‘intensity’ is a usefully amorphous concept to deploy; the kind of word you can drop into a list alongside ‘leaving too much space’ and ‘nobody closing down’ and call it punditry.

‘Intensity’ is hard to define because it sits at the cross-section between pressing systems and the psychological. Does a high-intensity midfield press invigorate players to believe in their own mental intensity, or do the players need to feel the intense high-confidence of a high-intensity coach to engage their pressing intensity? It’s almost as if the word has no meaning.

But the application of the word ‘intensity’ across the Premier League weekend just gone can be instructive. Chelsea haven’t got it. Nor do Manchester City. Tottenham Hotspur have it. Liverpool have got it, sometimes, and Arsenal – Arsenal always have it, even if a lot of people don’t want to see it.

If there is a serious tactical point to be made here, it’s about the Premier League as a fast and direct division and - although it might sound sacrilegious to say it – it’s about Pep Guardiola’s modern irrelevance.

The great man himself foresaw this years ago, when he famously mused that “modern football is not positional”, and is instead being defined by “riding the rhythm” like Bournemouth.

Only one of his disciples listened, the one who looks set to win back-to-back Premier League titles. The others are floundering.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Enzo Maresca and Xabi Alonso are both students of Guardiola, the former his assistant at Manchester City and the latter a mentee when playing under Pep at Bayern Munich. Both managers historically prefer very low-tempo possession football (in their title-winning season, Alonso’s Bayer Leverkusen had the slowest direct speed upfield in the Bundesliga, at 1.71 m/s), a hallmark of Guardiola’s suffocating tactical domination of English football across seven years.

But the era of Guardiola ended more than two years ago. Watching Chelsea and Man City play this season, it shows.

Chelsea’s 4-1 defeat to Leeds United followed a pattern of the campaign, in that Alonso’s side appear too soft, steady, and meticulous in their actions to cope with the Premier League’s physicality. Alonso’s rigid ‘positional play’ – demarcated positions, sideways passing, detailed instructions of where each pass should go – is pure Pep. It simply could not cope with Leeds’ man-to-man pressing.

The Premier League is a fast and direct division… the era of Guardiola ended more than two years ago

Leeds recorded more recoveries (51 to 39) and more pressures (508 to 416) than Chelsea, had a considerably lower PPDA (13 to 19) and forced twice as many high turnovers (15 to 7). Yes, Leeds had intensity; Chelsea did not.

Over at the Etihad, it was startling to see the hosts refuse to press Fulham’s defenders at all, instead sitting in a quiet midblock that allowed Alvaro Arbeloa’s side to build momentum. From this low-intensity starting position, City could not engage quickly when Fulham sprung a counter-attack.

Looking at the arc of history, we are currently between eras, perhaps, with Andoni Iraola and Roberto De Zerbi – now there’s intensity – likely to emerge as major players once Long Guardiola fades and “riding the rhythm” takes its place. But in the meantime, Arsenal are in dynasty territory thanks to Mikel Arteta, a Guardiola disciple who cast aside his tutor’s teachings long ago.

He is not given anywhere near enough credit for this.

On Saturday, sloppy mistakes are all that prevented Arsenal from seeing out a brilliantly masterminded victory at St James Park, where Arteta’s tactical instructions pulled the man-to-man Newcastle press out of shape, creating ‘artificial transitions’: build-up attacks that, by baiting a press and then turning it, give the illusion of a counter-attack.

Time and time again, Kai Havertz would pull short as the false nine to drag a centre-back with him, at which point Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke would make clever inverted runs into the space for longer Arsenal passes to hit. It was fast, sharp, and intense – and it led directly to both goals.

It was seriously smart, out-witting Matthias Jaissle’s ‘high-intensity’ football (from the Red Bull school) and proving, again, that Arteta is one of the best tacticians the Premier League has ever seen.

That is not a popular opinion, probably because people do not like the conservatism that has increasingly defined Arsenal’s attacking play, but also because the tactical complexity of what he does – the form of ‘intensity’ his football takes – does not conform to expectations.

Accusations of low intensity are generally a wishy-washy way of saying the plan isn’t working, highlighting a tactical problem without actually defining what it is. But in the cases of Alonso and Maresca, it is easy to diagnose once we watch Arsenal’s verticality, their directness, their urgency in picking apart Newcastle’s game plan.

As usual, Arteta is ahead of the curve, and he comes with a message for Alonso and Maresca: if you want to play with ‘intensity’, you must first let go of the master’s teachings.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

#781. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

With uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

#779. Smith: Paths align better for Stevenson unification than Azim fight

Dalton Smith has had an outstanding 2026, winning and defending the WBC super-lightweight world title with wins over Subriel Matias and Alberto Puello; Smith believes he can headline at Hillsborough Stadium in his Sheffield hometown with American star Shakur Stevenson a potential opponent

Dalton Smith, the WBC super-lightweight champion, thinks he's more likely to fight Shakur Stevenson next than Adam Azim.

Sheffield's Smith has had an outstanding year, knocking out Subriel Matias in New York to win his world championship and defending the belt against Alberto Puello in his Sheffield hometown.

American star Shakur Stevenson secured the WBO's super-lightweight championship when he beat Teofimo Lopez in January.

Both Smith and Stevenson are looking for their next opponents and a unification between the pair would be an appealing match up.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Boxing's business and if it makes good business on both sides it's definitely a fight that can be made. Obviously there's other champions, other belts. I just want to be part of the biggest fights," Smith told Sky Sports.

"It's a fight where the paths align a little bit better than me and Adam Azim right now. But like I said we'll see."

His advice to Azim is: "Be in world level fights.

"It's a fight what gets talked about a lot," Smith said of Azim. "I've got my own path I'm going on. I'm not just saying I'm doing. I think Adam needs to play his part as well.

"I'm not really concentrating on Adam. I'll let him do what he's doing.

"I'm concentrating on a big 2027 for me."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He would love to headline at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield next year.

"I'm in a position now to be part of some big, big fights," Smith said. "I'd love to have Hillsborough, I'd love to win more world titles.

"It's something I've dreamt of for years, I've always said it. People probably thought I was delusional at the time saying it, but I kept following the dream and I feel like it's very close. Possibly something we can get over the line next year. It'll just be big for Sheffield, big for the city and I'll be proud to say I've done it.

"I feel like I'm carrying that torch for the city now."

#778. Sutton's predictions v world champion boxer Lauren Price

Manchester United start life under new boss Mauricio Pochettino on Sunday but will they get their first Premier League win since August when they face Liverpool at Anfield?

"My worry for United is that they have one of the worst back fours in the Premier League," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Their defensive record is something Pochettino will try to address but, whoever he picks, they are just not very good."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers anad a variety of guests.

For week 11, he takes on boxer Lauren Price, who is an Arsenal fan.

She will defend her unified welterweight titles against Michaela Kotaskova on Friday, and has a shot at becoming Wales' first undisputed world champion after the vacant WBO welterweight title was added to the fight.

Price returns to home soil at the Utilita Arena in Cardiff for a fight that will be shown live on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer, from 21:00 GMT.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Price, the first Welsh boxer to be an amateur world champion and win Olympic gold, said: "When I turned pro it was my dream to become 'undisputed'. To achieve that and make history again for Wales on Friday, and in front of my own fans too, would be a dream come true."

Before turning to boxing, Price was a world kickboxing champion and international footballer - she captained the Wales Under-19 side, and played for the senior team as well as Cardiff City.

"My football days have helped me massively to get where I am in the ring today," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport.

"I honestly believe my footwork, and how fast my feet are, comes from when I played football.

"I am really proud of everything I achieved in football, especially playing for my country. It is the same now in boxing - to get in the ring and represent Wales is always an honour."

Price said the support of her grandparents helped her become successful at so many sports - and she followed her grandad, Derek, by becoming an Arsenal fan too.

"When I was a kid I was absolutely besotted with football and Arsenal were THE team when I was growing up," she explained.

"It was just the way they played under Arsene Wenger, and how they passed the ball - it was incredible. I loved Robin van Persie but Thierry Henry was my icon, my hero."

Chris Sutton and Lauren Price were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

The wheels have come off for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City with three Premier League defeats in a row.

It's not just City's results which have been alarming, either - they were well beaten by Nottingham Forest last time out, and their performance would have been the biggest concern for their manager.

In contrast, Fulham's results have improved of late and they are unbeaten in four league games. They've done all right whenever I've seen them this season, so I'm not surprised to see them picking up points.

Still, the international break probably came at a good time for Maresca to sort things out. Erling Haaland is scoring again too - not that he ever really stopped for very long - and I'm expecting City to be much better here.

I'm even going for them to keep a clean sheet, for the first time in eight games. I'm always brave... which is why I am bottom of the predictions table.

Lauren's prediction: City are having a tricky time of it at the moment but they should still win this. 2-0

I was at Sunderland's win over Chelsea and they thoroughly deserved it. They had been on a dreadful run of results before then, but it was a reminder of what they are about.

Brian Brobbey was just phenomenal for the Black Cats in that game but, like his captain Granit Xhaka, he is injured and will miss out here.

That just makes me think Aston Villa will have the edge. I always fancy them at home anyway with the way they go after teams, although I don't think this will be easy for them.

Villa boss Unai Emery was fuming after his side threw away a two-goal lead twice in their 4-4 draw at Manchester United, but they will hold on this time while Sunderland go down fighting.

Lauren's prediction: Villa are going really well. 2-1

Bournemouth have won eight games in a row in all competitions and it is incredible how Marco Rose has turned things around after a slow start.

The Cherries were absolutely flying before the international break - but will the two weeks off affect their momentum?

Forest did not need the break either, after their brilliant win over Manchester City.

That was such an important result for their manager Oliver Glasner but I think they will find it difficult to follow it up at Bournemouth.

Lauren's prediction: Forest shocked City last time out but I am going with Bournemouth here, they are on a brilliant run. 2-1

Chelsea were so lethargic when I watched them lose against Sunderland, and I don't think they were hard done by in that game - they looked flimsy at the back, and were deservedly beaten.

I had a bit of a pile-on from some Chelsea fans for saying that after the game, but then Xabi Alonso came out and was also heavily critical of the way they had defended - so he and I are on the same page there.

If Joao Pedro is fit then they will at least have more physicality up front this week, but I still have a feeling Leeds will get something out of this.

Daniel Farke's side got a great win over Tottenham last time out and they do not give much away - Arsenal and Brighton are the only top-flight teams to have conceded fewer league goals this season.

Leeds have definitely benefited from signing keeper James Trafford and what a move it has been for him personally as well.

I admire him for that, because he could have hung around at Manchester City as Gianluigi Donnarumma's number two, but he wanted first-team football. Now he is battling it out with Jordan Pickford to be England's number one.

Lauren's prediction: I don't think Leeds will keep Chelsea quiet. 3-1

This is the battle of the Franks... Lampard versus Thomas.

Thomas Frank's first conundrum as Crystal Palace's new manager is to stop them leaking so many goals - they have conceded 24 in their first 10 games, which is concerning.

I still think Palace have got some really good players, like Ismaila Sarr, Jorgen Strand Larsen and Jean-Philippe Mateta, and it's just a case of them getting fit and finding some form.

The way Coventry play, the Eagles are going to get some chances - but can they take them?

Frank Lampard's side counter-attack with such vigour, so I definitely think they will score... but I can see Palace's forward players having some joy too.

Lauren's prediction: I'm standing next to a Palace fan now, Ed from Boxxer, so I've got to go with them here! 0-2

We've seen Palace change their manager after making a disastrous start but they are still only four points below Ipswich and they will certainly see that as retrievable.

The Tractor Boys are not in the relegation zone but they are still in a relegation fight so, it is important for them to keep picking points up here and there. The trouble for them is that I don't see them getting anything at Tottenham.

Spurs lost to Leeds last time out but I still think they have turned a corner with their performances before that defeat.

I actually think this will be a routine win for Roberto de Zerbi's side, and I'm going for them to keep a clean sheet too.

Lauren's prediction: Spurs will take this one. 2-1

I am covering this game and I think it is a huge one for Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.

The Magpies have picked up as many points - 12 - in their first 10 games under Jaissle as they did when Eddie Howe was in charge last season, but I still don't think their fans are overly convinced by him.

Some of their unease is because Newcastle don't seem to have a defined style of play, and can be a bit kamikaze going forward.

Because of that, I just think Arsenal will pick them off, and win comfortably.

The Gunners have conceded only five league goals so far and have made an incredible start to their title defence with nine wins out of 10.

The worry for their rivals is that it feels to me Mikel Arteta's side have not even got going yet, but I still don't see anyone being close to them.

Lauren's prediction: No problems for Arsenal here! 0-4

Hull are going to scrap and fight - they have not won for eight games now, but they have still picked up some points because of their battling approach.

You know they will get in Brighton's faces but I don't think it will bother the Seagulls too much.

I want to apologise to Hull fans because I keep writing the Tigers off every week, but I am going to do it again here because Brighton are such a good team going forward and defensively.

Lauren's prediction: Brighton to edge this one. 0-1

Good luck to Pochettino. I like him as a manager and he seems a decent guy too.

He will need some luck as well, because it is going to be incredibly difficult for him to succeed at Old Trafford.

The constant for Manchester United is their managers keep getting the sack, when the club's problems seem to be deeper-lying than that.

Pochettino will get time because of what he has taken over, but it is amazing and also alarming to think United are in the bottom three, and could be bottom by the time this game is played.

As well as being so poor at the back, they have a midfield without any great athleticism and, stylistically, they did not really have an identity under Michael Carrick.

If you are Pochettino, you are probably going into the dressing room and putting your arm arm around Bruno Fernandes, to get the old sulker onside.

He really needs to, because Fernandes is an outstanding player and played a key role in the club's form with his numbers last season.

United need to see that version of him more than ever now, because so far this season he has not got going at all.

As for Liverpool, well I think they will get there under Andoni Iraola. It is just taking a bit of time for his players to adapt to his style.

They are not particularly fluid most of the time, and it feels like Iraola is not quite sure what his best midfield is.

Liverpool are still a work in progress, and United have picked up some results at Anfield recently - two draws and a win in their past three visits - but I can only see one result here, and it is a home victory.

Pochettino will probably look to defend and play on the counter-attack, and they might get some chances that way, but Liverpool are going to win. The only question is how many they will score.

Carrick began by beating Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games in January. Pochettino might start by being on the wrong end of a pummelling.

Lauren's prediction: Liverpool are at home and I am going with them to win it. 2-1

Brentford beat Everton 4-2 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium last season but, in three of their past four meetings, the points have been shared.

This has got a draw written all over it, too.

Everton are so solid under David Moyes, and so well organised, that I just don't see them losing. Brentford will keep things tight as well.

Lauren's prediction: Both these teams are doing well and this should be pretty even - I haven't gone for a draw yet, so let's finish with one. 1-1

Before the international break, Chris got four correct results with no exact scores from the 10 games in week 10, giving him 40 points.

His guests were the computer game Football Manager 27 and Miles Jacobson, the studio director of Sports Interactive, the company behind it.

Miles managed five correct results with no exact scores, giving him 50 points, while FM 27 got six correct results with three exact scores, to end up on 150 points.

Their individual totals will be shown on the guest leaderboard below - with FM 27 going top - but they have been combined, giving them an average of 100 points, for the guest score for the BBC predictions league table.

That means they miss out on the weekly win, which ended up in a tie between the BBC readers and AI. They both got six correct results with no exact scores, for a tally of 120 points.

There was only one game where everyone picked the right outcome - Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace.

Chris, FM 27, Miles, AI and the BBC readers all backed the Reds to win, but AI was the only one to get the score spot on.

There were two games where no-one got the correct result - Nottingham Forest's win over Manchester City, and Sunderland's victory against Chelsea.

Out of more than 25,000 predictions, fewer than 1,500 people thought Forest would beat City and only 36 of them got the 3-1 scoreline right too.

#777. Ayanna Howard thinks ‘everyone has to be part of’ building ethical AI tools

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Robotics researcher Ayanna Howard sees artificial-intelligence tools as an equalizer. Credit: Emma Parker Photography

Rebooting the Machines: A New Human Vision for Artificial Intelligence Ayanna Howard Broadleaf (2026)

As artificial-intelligence tools upend the graduate job market, it might seem that there’s little for educators to be optimistic about. But AI and robotics pioneer Ayanna Howard, who is the president of Spelman College, a historically Black women’s university in Atlanta, Georgia, sees promise ahead.

Howard’s career has ranged from developing autonomous robotic systems at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory to serving as dean of the college of engineering at Ohio State University. She is a co-founder of Zyrobotics, a company that creates educational technologies for children who need extra support, and academic co-lead of Black in Robotics, an organization dedicated to making the robotics field more inclusive.

In her book Rebooting the machines, Howard explains that the dangers of AI are real. Yet AI tools can improve people’s quality of life and create job opportunities — if humanity implements guard rails. She spoke to Nature about why she tells her students to embrace the technology, albeit with healthy scepticism.

I consider myself a realistic optimist. I’m positive about the possibilities of AI tools, but I realize that not everyone thinks the same way as I do — including some AI developers and companies in this space. We still need to do something to turn that optimistic viewpoint into reality.

If all types of individuals — those from various socio-economic backgrounds, races, genders and nationalities, and those that have disabilities, for example — all become part of the AI ecosystem, tools can be personalized. For instance, in health care, I want AI tools that are trained on my body composition, taking into account my age and the fact that I’m female. I don’t want a general model that was trained on men.

Honestly, I’m optimistic about jobs. AI tools make knowledge much more accessible. For smart individuals who have not been trained as, say, a computer scientist, AI is an equalizer.

My advice is to have a healthy scepticism towards AI, but also to work out how to use these tools in your discipline and for your passions. Jobs are changing. For students starting university this year, I guarantee that when they graduate, the jobs available to them will be different to those that exist now.

I think that there is some fear, frankly, because some recent graduates don’t have jobs thanks to AI models accelerating the eradication of early-career roles. But the graduates who do get hired are those who know how to work with the AI tools that companies are throwing at them.

The ones that some people call soft skills, although I call them hard skills because AI models can’t replicate them. One of them is human curiosity, which leads to creativity. Also, people are really good at learning things for the first time, whereas AI needs tonnes of data to work anything out. That means humans are really good at dealing with anomalies.

Robots can be useful educational tools for children who have extra support needs.Credit: BSIP/UIG/Getty

The other element is that many jobs still rely on human connection. AI tools are pretty useful for diagnosis in health care. But we still want a human to interpret the AI output and interact with us. Those jobs are going to be difficult to replace.

Studies have shown that the current generation of young people report high levels of loneliness, and yet they’re also more connected than previous generations. I think that at some point they will say, ‘you know what? I don’t like being lonely. I need human connection’. But if people feel that AI is making them less lonely — although there is evidence that it isn’t — there is a risk that they will take a long time to come to that realization.

The other risk is that people begin to trust AI tools too much. Because AI models are getting so good, there is a tendency not to question them. For example, if an AI tool used in health care tells people something incorrect and they don’t examine it, that could be disastrous.

The cost of hardware has gone down, and the time needed for a robot to learn what we call the action space — I see something, I work out how to do something and then I am able to actually do it physically — has shortened. That’s what’s required to operate in the real world.

You can’t ‘control–alt–delete’ harm to a human. With a virtual AI tool, if it completes a task, it’s not doing anything physically. (Although, as AI agents become more sophisticated, there’s a question of how much longer that will be the case.) Currently, a human still has to say ‘yes’, or confirm or click something to initiate a behaviour. When an AI model controls a physical system, you don’t necessarily have that feedback loop. That is a very risky scenario.

One answer is to collect more data. There are communities that don’t give their data to organizations training AI models because they know that their information could be used against them. But for applications that involve high risk but high return, we have to have a conversation about it. When a company tests a drug, people are willing to volunteer to take it and provide their data, because the benefits outweigh the risks. Can we do the same thing for some AI applications?

#776. Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024

#775. Commanders upset Burrow's Bengals after last-second winner

Drew Stevens kicks last-second field goal to lift Washington Commanders to surprise win over Joe Burrow's high-flying Cincinnati Bengals; watch an NFL Thanksgiving triple-header live on Sky Sports NFL from 5pm on ThursdaySky Sports

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jayden Daniels connected with rookie Antonio Williams on two long pass plays, moving the Commanders 64 yards in 34 seconds to set up Drew Stevens' 26-yard field goal as time expired as the Washington Commanders stunned Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals 22-20 on Monday night.

After Evan McPherson put the Bengals ahead 20-19 on a 56-yard field goal, Washington got the ball back with 39 seconds left and no timeouts.

Daniels hit Williams over the middle for 22 yards, spiked the ball, then found him again for a 42-yard catch-and-run to the Cincinnati eight. The Commanders quarterback spiked it with five seconds left and Stevens did the rest.

Daniels finished with 283 yards passing, Williams had nine catches for 122 yards, and Stevens was five for five on field goals as Washington (4-5-1) remained in the NFC East race, two games behind the division-leading New York Giants.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Burrow threw for 300 yards and two touchdowns for AFC North-leading Cincinnati (7-3), but the Commanders largely held in check a Bengals team that had won five straight, scoring 31 points or more each time.

Washington's defense forced Burrow to settle for checkdowns all night.

The dangerous Bengals receiving duo of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins combined for just seven catches for 74 yards.

Washington coach Dan Quinn made another questionable late-game decision when he sent Stevens out on fourth-and-one to kick a 41-yard field goal with 2:26 left for a 19-17 lead. That left plenty of time for Burrow, who found Mike Gesicki for a 32-yard completion to move the Bengals into field goal range.

A sack pushed the Bengals back, but McPherson nailed the long kick with 46 seconds remaining.

The game got off to a slow start in rainy conditions but opened up in the second half as the teams traded scores throughout the third quarter.

Burrow's four-yard touchdown pass to Colbie Young put the Bengals ahead 17-10, and the Commanders rallied with three field goals by Stevens.

There was an unexpected stoppage early in the third when the stadium lights went out with the Commanders in the red zone. After a delay that lasted about four minutes, Stevens converted from 36 yards to tie the game at 10-all.

Washington held Cincinnati to three points on its first four drives before Higgins' 31-yard touchdown catch that made it 10-0.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt, activated off injured reserve earlier Monday, scored on a one-yard run for the Commanders with 12 seconds left before halftime.

A Thanksgiving double-header of matches will also be shown live on Sky Sports on Thursday.

Chicago Bears travel to face Detroit Lions and the match is live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports NFL from 5pm on Thursday.

It will be followed by Philadelphia Eagles clash against Dallas Cowboys at 9pm, also on Sky Sports Main event and Sky Sports NFL.

#774. The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture

Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.

That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.

They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," said Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya said.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

#773. Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino's reign as Manchester United manager got off to a dismal start as his side were beaten 4-0 by rivals Liverpool after playing 82 minutes with 10 men.

Here's how BBC Sport rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below.

Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6

Ronald Araujo: Never really tested defensively. Made a few contributions going forward. 7

Jeremy Jacquet: Went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo in the box at 0-0, although a penalty against the French defender would have been harsh. 6

Virgil van Dijk: Organised the defence well. Also had a header well-saved at 0-0 and nodded another wide in the second half. 7

Milos Kerkez: Always keen to drive Liverpool up the pitch. Had some nice link-ups with Rio Ngumoha. 7

Dominik Szoboszlai: Fantastic driven free-kick to open the scoring. Went close a few more times with long shots and generally bossed the midfield. 8

Alexis Mac Allister: Did all the simple things right and allowed others to shine around him. Forced Senne Lammens into a top save in the first half. 7

Bradley Barcola: Missed a few chances to score his first league goal for Liverpool when through one-vs-one. Showed his electric pace to set up his side's third. 7

Florian Wirtz: Readjusted well to net Liverpool's second and assisted their fourth. Five goals in four games for club and country now and looks close to his creative best. 8

Rio Ngumoha: So direct and skilful. Scored Liverpool's third with a calm finish. Also set up their second after easily beating Diogo Dalot. Club and country have a real talent on their hands. 9

Alexander Isak: Led the line well but missed some big chances. Won the free-kick that resulted in Szoboszlai's goal and led to Leny Yoro's sending off. 6

Victor Munoz (on 72, Barcola): Good cameo and took his goal well, curling it into the far corner. 7

Trey Nyoni (on 72, Mac Allister): Looked bright. Had a shot go just over. 6

Subs not used: Chiesa, Mamardashvili, McConell, Tsimikas.

Senne Lammens: Could he have done better with the opener? Good save to deny Mac Allister and some decent stops after that. 6

Leny Yoro: Did he have to make the tackle on Isak? It was almost as though he thought about whether he should and decided the answer was yes. Given Liverpool scored from the free-kick it was a bad decision. 4

Matthijs de Ligt: First Premier League start in almost 12 months in middle of a back three turned into a nightmare with the early error that led to opening goal and Yoro red card. Struggled from that moment on. 4

Lisandro Martinez: Fully extended by Liverpool's attack. The least bad of the visitors' starting defence, but that isn't saying much. Exposed completely by Barcola for Liverpool's third. 5

Diogo Dalot: Given a torrid time by Ngumoha, which prompted Pochettino to bring on Maguire. Tries hard but it's not enough. 5

Youri Tielemans: Concerns about a midfield partnership with Mainoo emerge again. Not having the sustained impact required for a player of his experience. 4

Kobbie Mainoo: Twenty-one-year-old being asked to shoulder so much responsibility in an ailing team. New midfield recruits have not helped him. 5

Bryan Mbeumo: Couple of decent bursts came to nothing, then sacrificed after Yoro red card. Received consoling pat on the head from his new boss. 5

Bruno Fernandes: Early free-kick just wide and shot straight at Alisson. Given the carnage at Old Trafford this season, no wonder contract talks on hold. Furious at free-kick given against him when he thought he was through. 5

Patrick Dorgu: Asked to do an awful lot, initially as wing-back, then further back. Lucky Barcola fluffed his lines or his failure to keep an offside line would have been exposed. 5

Matheus Cunha: Tried to keep simmering frustration in check. Not easy in a losing side with no service. Replaced at the break. 5

Harry Maguire (on 22, Mbeumo): Couldn't have expected to be called on so soon. Went into middle of back three and immediately blocked an Isak effort to prevent a third goal. Tried hard. 5

Joshua Zirkzee (on 46, Cunha): Pre-match rumours of a rare start proved unfounded. Replaced Cunha at half-time and asked to bring a different skillset to the number nine role. More physical but not as good and lost possession too easily. 4

Mason Mount (on 65, Tielemans): Only on for a couple of minutes when attempted crossfield pass went to Liverpool player and eventually a third goal. 5

Noussair Mazraoui (on 65, Dorgu): Not really sure what he was supposed to do. Tried to push forward as United's poor control brought more pressure. 4

Subs not used: Heaton, Amad Diallo, Heaven, Lacey.

#772. Holders Celtic win 17-0 in Women's Scottish Cup

Isabella Fisher scored four goals in Celtic's win

Holders Celtic breezed through to the fourth round of the Women's Scottish Cup with a 17-0 victory over Forfar Farmington.

Morgan Cross and Casey Howe both netted hat-tricks, Isabella Fisher scored four times and Amy Gallacher bagged a double.

Lauren Doran-Barr, Addie Handley, Maria McAneny and Evie Rabjohn also scored and Forfar conceded an own goal.

Last season's beaten finalists, Rangers, were 5-0 victors at home to Motherwell.

Mijke Roelfsema opened the scoring with her first Rangers goal, Eilidh Austin made it two and Laura Berry converted a penalty shortly before going off injured.

Fallon Connolly-Jackson got her maiden Rangers goal early in the second half and Hannah Blake completed the scoring.

Glasgow City defeated Cambusdoon 10-0. Leah Lane scored her first City goal, with Kelly Brady, Lisa Forrest, Abi Harrison, Yuuka Kurosaki, Jesi Rossman and Emily Whelan also on target.

Sofia Maatta netted twice and Cambusdoon conceded an own goal.

Reigning Scottish champions Heart of Midlothian won 6-0 away to Stenhousemuir.

Lucy Jane Hope put the visitors in front and Jenny Smith doubled their lead. Ava Crawford got the third, Monica Forsyth also netted and Hope and Forsyth added to the tally.

Montrose won 13-0 at Dunipace, with Neve Guthrie, Kaela McDonald-Nguah and Hannah Stewart each scoring once, Francesca Ogilvie netting twice, Darcie Miller bagging a hat-trick and Demi Taylor picking up a four-goal haul, with an own goal also aiding the visitors.

Spartans were 11-2 winners at home to Bonnyrigg Rose. Zara Andrews and Ronaigh Douglas both scored once, there were doubles for Emily Cadell, Tegan Reynolds and Izzy Young, while Emma McMurdo scored a hat-trick.

Mya Christie, Holly Daniel, Christie again and Briana Salvetti all netted in Aberdeen's 4-0 home win over Dryburgh Athletic.

SWPL2 side Boroughmuir Thistle won 2-1 on penalties against top-flight Partick Thistle after a 1-1 draw. Imogen Longcake gave the visitors a second-half lead, but Amy Denholm levelled to force extra time.

Falkirk were 7-0 winners at home to Renfrew. Maisy Stewart, Skye Neillie, Mhari Smith, Caitlin McFarlane and Olivia Murphy all scored first-half goals, with McFarlane and Emma Lawson adding to the rout after the break.

Queen's Park beat Dundee United 2-1, with Ellie Kane and Darcy Molloy putting the hosts two up at the break and Lucy Stevenson replying in the second half.

Rossvale won 3-2 at home to Gartcairn. Maddie Wilson and Sarah Petherick had Rossvale 2-0 up, but Clare Docherty replied for the visitors before the break. Petherick's second proved to be the winner, with Gartcairn's Madison Maxwell netting a late consolation.

#771. Wolves are clicking, Stoke are dreaming - but could QPR be dark horses?

Wolves are improving defensively, Stoke look strong and QPR look resolute; Andy Hinchcliffe picks out the key stories in The Championship catch-up; a Sky Sports column focusing on the second tier.

Welcome to The Championship Catch-up, a new Sky Sports column in which Andy Hinchcliffe rounds up some of the key stories from the second tier. This week:

With the players Wolves have got and the way they play, they were always going to score goals. They've averaged around 1.7 goals per game across those periods, so they're still good for a goal under Cesar Peixoto.

But in the last seven games they've conceded only five, compared to the 14 goals they shipped in their first nine. They're not playing defensively, they're just defending well. They're keeping the ball and keeping teams away from their penalty area.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

At the start of the season they were too open. They were great to watch and scoring goals, but conceding too many. They needed to find a balance. They didn't have to become ultra-defensive, but they did need some defensive strength.

They've got plenty of attacking threats. Raul Jimenez is still missing, but Adam Armstrong is doing really well and is a proven goalscorer at this level. They've got width, dynamism and options, while Andre plays a really important role sitting deep in midfield.

All I was looking for was more balanced performances. They didn't need to let the goals dry up just to keep clean sheets. They've managed to find that balance and do both. They're dominating games, keeping teams out and still scoring goals.

Even when they change the right-back, centre-half or left-back, they can maintain that defensive strength. They're clearly moving in the right direction and are now a much more balanced, complete team.

Kieran Trippier's experience has been invaluable. He cares about the club getting promoted back to the Premier League. Individually, he wants to do well, but he also wants the team to succeed.

He's perhaps not the player he was five years ago, but he can still have a huge effect. He'll have to get used to the fact that he might not play every game, but Wolves have the depth to manage that.

With Trippier, it's not just about his ability but also his leadership and experience. He can reinforce the standards they should be setting and what they're looking to achieve this season.

Stoke City have won 10 of 16 games, more than any other Championship team. Would you have expected them to have won more games than Wolves, West Ham, Middlesbrough or Southampton after 16 matches? Probably not.

They're still overachieving in terms of the data, but Mark Robins spoke during the international break about the need to improve their performances. The league position doesn't really tell you how good you are. You have to monitor performances and look at how to develop and improve.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

There's still work to do at both ends of the pitch, but they're getting goals from different players. George Hirst came in for big money and had been struggling for goals and not starting games. He won them the game against Birmingham, which is a lift for him and the team.

Against Birmingham, they were down to 10 men for a long time and showed the resilience to hold on to a 1-0 lead. When you look at everything, the foundations are there for them to get better.

How many experienced, very good coaches have gone to Stoke and not been able to make it work? We all hoped Mark Robins would succeed because of the work he did at Coventry, but there was always the question of whether he would become another coach who fell foul of a club where nobody seemed able to get things going.

I just think it's wonderful that it's him because he's such a brilliant coach. He's very understated and humble. I saw him after a game recently and asked him a couple of tactical questions. He was saying he was glad I'd noticed certain things he'd done. He's very engaging, but it's not all about him. It's about the job he's there to do.

Player for player, this Stoke side is better than last season's team. That's what I'm saying about their recruitment and the shape Mark is playing. They're better, and the fact they can improve further makes things look really positive.

But we're only 16 games into a long season. Mark will know winter is really tough for every team, particularly when you're up near the top and everyone is looking to knock you off your position. They'll be looking at their performances and adjusting their training because that's all you can do.

Could Stoke possibly be in the mix for a top-two finish? With the way they're playing and the players they've got, who could improve further, very possibly.

Defensively for QPR there's been the big shift this season. They were 23rd last season for goals conceded and are now in the top four. That's the foundation. If you don't concede too many goals in the Championship, you've got a chance.

I don't think they're a defensive team. They're a team that defend well. It doesn't mean they're sitting everybody behind the ball and playing on the counter-attack. They can dominate possession and force opponents backwards. They defend well, but they're not defensive.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jimmy Dunne, Ronnie Edwards and Pierce Charles are absolutely crucial, but the team structure is there too. They've got a solid base and the nice problem now is working out how to be more creative.

It was important to win at Millwall and maintain their momentum in the top eight, but they won't always find themselves in such a dominant position. There's still work to do going forward to become more threatening and dangerous.

They need to find a regular goalscorer, but they also need to create more chances. Getting Ilias Chair back into the team regularly is important. He's one of those players who can affect games in the Championship.

This has to be a big season for Chair. He undoubtedly has the ability, but at times he's coasted along and hasn't become the dominant force Rangers need him to be.

If they want to improve going forward and finish in the top eight, he's key. He's got the movement, intelligence and creative quality, and he can score goals. It's not just about what he can do himself, but what he can do for the players around him.

Looking at his performance against Millwall and what he could bring for the rest of the season, I think he's key to improving their attack. It's down to him to drive that improvement.

#770. 'Rolls-Royce' Iqbal's 'dream' journey from Old Trafford to Tannadice

Jim Goodwin's side are eight games unbeaten, with Zidane Iqbal pivotal

Given the superlatives being thrown in the direction of Zidane Iqbal by the Scottish football fraternity, one would think he was a replica of a certain France great instead of just sharing his name.

So much so that BBC Radio Scotland pundits were suggesting on Saturday's Sportsound that the 23-year-old is the answer to Celtic's hunt for a long-term successor to captain Callum McGregor as their midfield general.

It is just as well for Dundee United that the Iraq international is tied to them until at least the summer, his early season appearances for Utrecht ruling out a transfer during the January window.

So, where has he sprung from and what is all the fuss about?

Hibs 0-4 Dundee United: What Goodwin said

Born in Manchester to a Pakistani father and an Iraqi mother, Iqbal came through the Old Trafford youth system.

He signed his first professional contract with United in 2021 and became the first British-born South Asian and first-ever British South Asian to play in the Champions League when he came on as an 89th-minute substitute against Young Boys that December.

However, that was to be his one and only first-team appearance and, although he had already made his international debut in a World Cup qualifier at the age of 19, he was sold to Utrecht for a reported fee of Â£1m in summer 2023.

Starting off in their Jong Utrecht second string, he would go on to make 49 appearances for the Dutch top-flight outfit before making a surprise switch to the Scottish Premiership this summer.

On the one hand, United were getting a player who played all three of Iraq's games at this summer's World Cup, two of them starts, albeit all three were heavy defeats.

On the other hand, Iqbal had only managed seven appearances last season for Utrecht and had been a second-half substitute in two of their four matches at the start of the new campaign.

However, after a pivotal display in what was being described as a midfield "masterclass" by United in Saturday's 4-0 dismantling of hosts Hibernian, manager Jim Goodwin revealed he always had belief the Tangerines were unearthing a "Rolls-Royce".

"The head of recruitment's job is to go and identify good talent for us," Goodwin told BBC Scotland. "It's my job to give him the profile and then he goes out and does the groundwork.

"We could see immediately when we watched the footage of Zidane and when we had the Zoom call with him and his representatives, we not only had a fantastic player but a really good person with the right characteristics to come and fit the culture here."

Zidane Iqbal was also a marked man at the World Cup finals

While on-loan Rangers man Lyall Cameron was among the goals and fellow 24-year-old Dylan Tait provided a stylish assist, it was the third leg of what some regard as the best midfield triumvirate in the Premiership who was singled out for most praise at Easter Road.

With former Celtic winger Aidan McGeady again pondering the question about McGregor's likely successor, transfer market expert and former United wing-back Allan Preston opined: "A six for Celtic? Look no further than young Iqbal.

"He's been magnificent since he's come to Scottish football, absolutely brilliant. Running the show again.

"If Celtic are looking for a young boy at his age with experience, he is a full international, knows the game, played in Scotland, you can see what he can do, there's your man in front of you.

"Other players' hair's on fire, but he's just nice and calm. He's at a different level. He doesn't panic. When the ball comes to him, he is so calm on it, he takes his time, he's got great peripheral vision."

The former Dundee United wing-back pointed out, though: "He's had his two clubs that he can play for in a year of football, so he is going nowhere until at least the summer, so enjoy him while you can because I think you'll get serious money for this young boy."

McGeady pointed to Iqbal's "good pedigree", having started with Manchester United and already having 32 caps for Iraq, but wondered if that would be enough for Celtic to consider him.

"I don't even think, if he's performing this well, Celtic will go and get him," said McGeady.

"Why are Celtic not looking at players like this? Do they feel they have to prove themselves somewhere else first?"

Former Celtic captain Scott Brown was similarly impressed.

"He's been a delight to watch - sharpness to get on the ball and willingness to drive forward," the former midfielder and manager pointed out.

"He beats a man in the middle of the park as well and there's not too many midfielders willing to do that.

"Watching him there talking to the media, he can't get the smile off his face. He enjoys football, he takes the ball under pressure, he does things that other people don't do, especially in midfield.

"He brings composure, but he can also drive through as well. His willingness to keep getting on the ball, even if he makes that slight mistake - that's what I really enjoy watching about him."

While Goodwin reckons there will be likely interest in the summer, Iqbal has no thoughts of so quickly leaving a club - and manager - who have resurrected his club career.

"I'm not even looking at any other clubs," he told BBC Scotland. "I'm fully focused on Dundee United.

"They've given me a platform to enjoy myself and play football. I'm really enjoying my football again.

"They've given me faith and confidence. The gaffer and the coaching staff have a lot of belief in me.

"The bare minimum I can do is pay them back with strong performances and hopefully it carries on."

Iqbal recalled being at Manchester United's "development centre since I was four or five - I signed when I was eight", explaining that he "then left for some first-team football".

He stressed that his lack of games last season came as a result of "a couple of injuries" and, while "I learnt a lot in Holland", he is "happy to have left that behind me", adding: "That book's closed now."

Visit our Dundee United page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

Get Dundee United news notifications in the BBC Sport app

Iqbal also recalled how Goodwin's enthusiasm persuaded him to make the switch to Tannadice on deadline day.

"After the World Cup, I had one year left on my contract and I was in touch with my agent," the midfielder said. "We both wanted a move and I had a few chats with a few clubs.

"To be fair, I left it a bit late for Dundee United, but after the first call with the gaffer, I straight away called my agent after we ended the call.

"I said, 'look, I genuinely feel like the guy really believes in me'.

"It happened very late. I had to drive from Holland to Scotland. It was a tough drive but worth it in the end."

That World Cup was also a defining experience, with representing his country in the United States described as surreal.

"Having your friends and family there to watch you and playing on the world stage, with so many people, was a dream," he said.

"Playing against top players gave me that confidence boost I needed. I thought I did well in the three tough games.

"I knew, wherever I'd end up, with the faith of the gaffer, I could really kick on and push because I've learnt so much from the World Cup."

Goodwin is the manager to have done that and Iqbal added: "He's such a top guy, not just in football.

"His tactics are amazing. Everyone's comfortable. Everyone wants to fight for him."

#769. Pepe did not injure eyes staring at sun, say Villarreal

Nicolas Pepe (right) wore an eye mask on his return to the side following his eye operation in October

Villarreal say reports striker Nicolas Pepe needed eye surgery because he stared directly at the solar eclipse are "completely false".

In a statement, the Spanish club said an operation in October that ruled the 31-year-old out for six matches was "scheduled in advance" and "entirely unrelated" to the eclipse, which took place on 12 August.

Reports on social media suggested the former Arsenal forward had injured his eyes staring directly at the sun during the lunar event, with a video then emerging - purportedly from one of Pepe's social media accounts - showing him watching it in Spain.

"Villarreal CF, in response to reports published in various media outlets recently, clarifies that it is completely false that Nicolas Pepe's eye surgery has any connection to viewing the solar eclipse," said the club.

"The surgery had been scheduled in advance for reasons entirely unrelated to this event.

"The club urges accuracy and responsibility when reporting on matters related to its players' health."

Staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

In the build-up to this summer's event, experts warned only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

Ivory Coast international Pepe has scored 14 goals in 86 appearances in all competitions for Villarreal after joining from Trabzonspor in 2024.

He cost Arsenal a then-club record Â£72m when he joined from Lille in the summer of 2019.

Pepe scored 27 goals in 112 games for the Gunners and had a loan spell at Nice before joining Trabzonspor on a free transfer.
