#748. The red card that changed Liverpool-Man Utd: correct call?

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.

It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.

Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?

Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Photographers at Anfield captured the sequence of events - from challenge to red card

Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.

Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.

Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.

Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.

There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:

distance between the offence and the goal

likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball

location and number of defenders and attackers

As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.

The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".

The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.

The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.

The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.

If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.

It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.

Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.

Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.

Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.

"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.

"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."

But for Liverpool boss Iraola the decision is not up for debate.

"I think he's the last man, no?" he said. "It's a clear foul and a red card, yes?

Did Liverpool 'get lucky' with red card decision?

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes felt it should not have been a red card and said the decision had a detrimental impact on the game.

"It's one that needs to be looked at," Fernandes told Sky Sports.

"We have far too many meetings with the referees for this to happen to us again. The last one against Chelsea [when Lisandro Martinez was sent off], you can give it as a red card and it was probably a second yellow also. Today, you can't give a red card.

"It's very clear they show us if the player is not in control of the ball, it's never a red card.

"Isak kicks the ball forward, the ball goes into the hands of Senne. Isak has got no control of the ball, he has no chance to get on the ball. He puts his leg across to try to get some advantage from Leny. I can understand the fall, but it's never a red card.

"There are too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR taking so long to see to make a mistake like this that can change the game.

"It's not because of them we conceded the goal from the free-kick, but it changes the game completely."

Pochettino, meanwhile, was frustrated by what he perceived as inconsistency in the decision-making of the officials.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss felt his new team should have been awarded a penalty moments before Yoro was sent off, after Jeremy Jacquet went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo.

"It's difficult to accept that because it was a foul under my view and for me was a penalty," Pochettino told Match of the Day.

"Look how everything changes if that action was a red card and a foul, I think we need to review. When I played football that situation is normal. The action against Mbeumo, if that [Yoro foul on Isak] was a red card then that was a penalty."

'We have too many referees' - Fernandes disagrees with Yoro red

There have been a couple of very similar cases this season.

Brighton's Pascal Struijk was sent off at Sunderland through a VAR review after he brought down Wilson Isidor.

The Seagulls successfully appealed against that red card on the grounds that there was clear doubt that Isidor would have taken control of the ball before it ran through to goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

Could Manchester United appeal against Yoro's red card? There's nothing to lose by doing so.

Despite the Football Association regulatory commission unanimously ruling the Struijk red card was wrong, the Premier League's key match incidents panel voted the VAR intervention was a correct call on a split 3-2 vote.

Ipswich's Issa Diop avoided a VAR red card for a foul on James McAtee against Nottingham Forest, when the referee disagreed with the video official, and believed there was a covering defender. Forest boss Oliver Glasner was adamant it had been a clear goalscoring opportunity.

It was the same referee, Thomas Bramall, for both of those incidents.

That shows just how subjective such decisions can be. It is often rare to get a real consensus.

Yoro can count himself a little unfortunate to get the red card.

#747. Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."

This article was originally written in German.

#746. Will Smith, Jada Pinkett Smith's $42 Million Estate Catches on Fire

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's $42 million Calabasas home was the site of an accidental shed fire Nov. 23, the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff's Station said.

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith had a scary moment at home.

A fire broke out on couple's $42 million property in Calabasas, Calif., in the early hours of Nov. 23 the Los Angeles County Fire Department confirmed, adding that authorities were able to contain the situation before it engulfed the estate.

"On November 23, 2026 at approximately 12:04 AM, deputies from the Malibu/Lost Hills Station responded to a report of a structure fire," the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff's Station said in a statement given to E! News. "Security at the location reported a maintenance shed was on fire. Upon arrival, deputies saw a shed type of structure engulfed in flames."

"Los Angeles County Fire Department personnel arrived and extinguished the fire," the statement continued. "No other structures were damaged, and no one was injured. The cause of the fire was accidental."

E! News has reached out to reps for Will and Jada and have yet to hear back.

The scary moment came days after the couple—who share kids Jaden Smith, 28, and Willow Smith, 26—stepped out for a rare family outing together.

Their moms Caroline Bright and Adrienne Banfield-Norris also took part in the daytime trip to Soho House’s Little Beach House Malibu in Malibu, Calif., on Nov. 21.

Though the couple—who quietly separated in 2016—have maintained a rather low profile in recent years, they have stepped out on several occasions to publicly show their support for their kids.

In June, the pair were joined by Willow, Adrienne and Will’s son Trey—whom he shares with ex Sheree Zampino—for a joint appearance at Paris Fashion Week to attend the Menswear Spring/Summer 2027 show for Christian Louboutin, which Jaden serves as the brand’s men’s creative director for.

During the trip to the fashion capital, the pair enjoyed a night out with Jaden, linking arms as they stepped out for dinner.

Though it’s been over a decade since the Bad Boys actor and Girls Trip star separated, Jada—who publicly revealed the breakup in 2023—shared that she and Will don’t plan on filing for divorce in the future.

As she told NBC News in 2023, “I made a promise that there will never be a reason for us to get a divorce.”

For a look back at Will and Jada’s relationship over the years, keep reading…

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith were all smiles at the Devil in a Blue Dress premiere in 1995.

Have you ever seen anything more '90s glam than this? The couple posed together in 1997, the year they got married.

Jada was styling more than just a trendy silver coat in this 1998 red carpet photo—she was also showing off her baby bump in a sleek black dress. The couple's son Jaden Smith was born on July 8, 1998.

During Jada's second pregnancy with daughter Willow Smith in 2000, Will couldn't help but to cradle the actress' baby belly at a celebrity boxing match in Los Angeles.

Hats off to the couple who never cease to show up on a red carpet in style. Here they were together at Hollywood's Kodak Theater in 2005.

Jada ignored the old superstition of never wearing to black to a wedding as she and Will headed to Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise's 2006 nuptials in Rome.

The kids were here in London with Will and Jada on the red carpet at The Karate Kid premiere in 2010.

Orange you glad to see this picture of Will and Jada together? The pair got cozy during an event in New York City in 2010.

Willow, Jaden, Will and Jada posed together in a family shot at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2012.

Jada dazzled in green as she and Will arrived at the 2016 Golden Globe Awards at the Beverly Hilton Hotel.

Everyone was all smiles for a family vacation after making a quick pit stop at the 2018 World Cup.

In 2020, the couple addressed Jada's alleged affair with August Alsina.

Admitting she and August had an "entanglement" while she and Will were separated, she explained, "It was a relationship. I was in a lot of pain and I was very broken. In the process of that relationship I definitely realized you can't find happiness outside of yourself. Luckily enough, you and I were also going through a process of healing in a much different manner."

During the 2022 Academy Awards, Will slapped host Chris Rock over a joke the comedian made about Jada's shaved head.

After the slap, Will resigned from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences and was banned from its events for 10 years. He also apologized to Chris, calling the slap "unacceptable" and noting "there is no part of me that thinks that was the right way to behave in that moment."

In October 2023, Jada revealed she and Will had been separated for seven years, including the six leading up to the 2022 Oscars.

"We're still figuring it out," Jada told People. "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

#745. Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford

Gino Pozzo (left) has presided over 25 permanent Watford bosses in 14 years, with Alessio Dionisi the latest to take charge of the Hornets

A week is said to be a long time in football, and few clubs offer a more compelling test of that theory than Watford.

It has been 14 years since the Pozzo family completed their takeover of the Hornets and Alessio Dionisi's dismissal leaves them searching for the 25th permanent boss of their tenure.

The Italian's dismissal was announced on Sunday lunchtime with his 18th and final game in charge proving to be the 4-0 defeat by Sheffield United less than 24 hours earlier.

An average incumbency of about 210 days per manager has generated all too familiar headlines of the Hornets seeking a new face in the dugout, but is there method in the madness?

Pozzo court case in Spain adds to unrest at Watford

Brereton Diaz double leads Blades to win over Watford

The Hornets were taken over by the Pozzos on 29 June 2012, with the family having also owned Serie A side Udinese since 1986.

Gino Pozzo has been in charge ever since, overseeing an ownership model rooted in a vast global scouting network famed for buying low and selling high, with Brazil internationals Richarlison and Joao Pedro among those flipped for big fees.

In the 61-year-old's first seven years, the club shifted from existential crisis to FA Cup finalists.

Under Javi Gracia, they came close to qualifying for Europe through the Premier League in 2019 before arriving at a Wembley showpiece where they came up second best to Manchester City.

But it proved to be a peak from which they have steadily spiralled.

Relegation from the Premier League a year later was followed by an immediate return - but a further relegation from which they have not recovered.

Last season's 16th-place finish was their lowest in the second tier under Pozzo - with a frequent turnover of manager seemingly utilised as a failed antidote to their stagnation.

That sense of inertia - and a poor start to 2026-27 which has left them 21st in the Championship, has brightened the spotlight on the owner and his methods.

With more than a third of the league season complete, Watford are one place outside of the Championship relegation zone

After back-to-back hammerings by Burnley and Cardiff City in October, former Hornets midfielder Tom Ince said he feared for the club he left at the end of last season.

"There are a lot of different beliefs on how the football club should move forward." Ince told the 72+ podcast.

He pointed to Gracia ending his second spell in charge last season after only three months - and with the club four points off the Championship play-offs - as a "big, big problem" that summed up their instability.

"There is so much control away from the manager at that club that it will always be an issue," said Ince. "The players don't see the manager as the focal point. He [Pozzo] is the one in control.

"That is always going to be a problem because you can't look at a manager and not have any fear [in them].

"I look at Watford, the players in the dressing room. You have a lot of young players, who have not played in England before. When this hiring and firing of managers is going on, they're just like 'OK, onto the next one [manager]'."

While Ince, now at League Two side Tranmere Rovers, added his respect for positives to Pozzo's practise, he is not alone in speaking out about the board's influence.

Speaking on No Tippy Tappy Football,, external former England boss Sam Allardyce said he had turned down the chance to manage the club prior to the appointment of Nigel Pearson in 2019.

"I got interviewed at Watford before Nigel [Pearson]," Allardyce revealed.

"[Sir] Elton [John] rang me up and said, 'Come on, Sam, take the job'.

"It was very nice having a phone call from Elton John, I must admit. But I met with the board, sat in the boardroom, and went, 'I can't take this job'.

"They were telling me what to do, saying, 'Play this way, play that player, this manager's not been playing that player' and so on."

Gino Pozzo has been Watford's owner since 2012

Ince and Allardyce's remarks came after former Watford owner John said he was "upset and disappointed" by the club's form after their 4-0 defeat by Burnley.

"I really feel for the supporters who have to watch this," he wrote in response to a club post on Instagram.

When supporter group The 1881 Movement published an open letter declaring a "complete loss of confidence" in Pozzo, the Italian, who has rarely spoken publically had no choice but to.

His meeting with prominent supporter Roy Moore was recorded and released as an extraordinary 114-minute podcast episode by the club's official channels.

Watford fans state 'loss of confidence' in ownership

Elton John 'upset and disappointed' with Watford form

"I don't have a social presence, I don't like to speak publicly, I don't enjoy that, I don't think it's productive for the work we do," Pozzo explained.

"I don't like to answer to speculation, because a lot of the people that are out there want a bit of visibility for themselves. Unfortunately social media creates this sort of character.

"I'm not expecting everybody to understand our model. In order to compete with the other clubs, we need to be something different. Otherwise we would not even be in the Championship right now."

Though Udinese is formally owned by his father, Giampaolo, Pozzo is still heavily involved in the management of the Italian club.

It is for this reason that he dismisses a reputation for devouring head coaches - Udinese boss Kosta Runjaic was, until his sacking earlier this month,, external Serie A's longest-serving manager having been appointed before the 2024-25 season.

"I tend to have a very good relationship with the coach, because the coach is a fundamental part," said Pozzo. "Whenever we sign a coach there is normally strong bond and good idea and we share that.

"It [sacking managers] has cost me a lot, I know I'm not looking good. Every time I change a coach, it's not a good image. But I cannot stand the fact that my image is worth more than the club's results. I put the club in front."

Watford have finished outside the top 10 in each of their past four Championship seasons

Before the win over Charlton Athletic on 17 October, some supporters tried to orchestrate a protest against Pozzo's ownership.

It is a far cry from the high point of his reign, when a tifo bearing his name was unfurled at Vicarage Road.

Tom Bodell, a Hornets supporter who contributes to the Watford Buzz podcast, said outside views of the club being a "basket case" who change manager two or three times a season was "the tip of the iceberg".

"We've seen over certainly three years, possibly five years now, a real reduction in overheads and outlay on the football side," he said.

"This summer we saw quite a bit of talent leave for reasonable money and next to nothing spent. We paid a fee for the goalkeeper Federico Ravaglia, but I believe that was it.

"Everybody else was either a loan, a free transfer or came from Udinese. So, you know, passing money from one pocket to the other on the same pair of jeans."

Bodell said chief executive and chairman Scott Duxbury had failed to deliver on promises of signing players with proven EFL experience, with concerns also mounting over the downgrading of the club's academy.

"There have been enough instances now of supporters feeling that they've been at best let down, at worst kind of misled or lied to that it is very hard to rebuild that trust," said Bodell.

"They [the owners] are at very real risk of leaving us in a worse position than when they arrived and I think that is probably the thing that has tipped people into action."

Alessio Dionisi lost more than half of his games in charge of Watford

But while the optics of Pozzo's model and methods have hit an all-time low for English observers, his image in his homeland is assured, according to Vincenzo Credendino, a journalist with Sport Italia.

"The [Pozzo] business model is a winning model because he is not an American billionaire or an Arab Sultan, he has to apply the model he worked on to buy young players and sell them," said Credendino.

"This is a model that allows Gino Pozzo with Udinese to compete in the Champions League, and reaching high levels at least in Italian football.

"If you look at many teams in Serie A, you can find many players who came out from Udinese. Piotr Zielinski, at Inter Milan is just one example."

For the frustration of Hornets' fans, it is a point that is difficult to deny.

Rodrigo de Paul, Alexis Sanchez, Alex Meret and Juan Cuadrado are all examples of players bought low and sold high at Udinese.

While at Watford, Abdoulaye Doucoure and Odion Ighalo are further examples of players to bring money into the Hertfordshire club.

"When you speak about Gino Pozzo, you are speaking about a piece of history." added Credendino.

"He's really pioneering. He has visions of the future. He has agreed a new perspective about many things, and many clubs look at his model and decided to make something similar."

So, is there method in the madness? Undoubtedly. But for those associated with Watford, the madness alone might prove to be Pozzo's lasting legacy.

#743. I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide - Pressley

Steven Pressley says there is a "fragility" in the Dundee squad

Head coach Steven Pressley has admitted that "at times, I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide" after Dundee's 8-0 "humiliation" by Heart of Midlothian.

Two days after the Dens Park debacle, Pressley is still adamant he must shoulder the blame - despite winger Alan Forrest earlier saying the "freak" result was down to the players.

Pressley said after the game he was concerned a poor result was imminent and admits he had sensed some complacency within the squad.

"Our strength has been built on cohesion, unity and aggressiveness," said the head coach, who said he was embarrassed by the result but that at difficult times he "seems to find strength from somewhere".

"I think Saturday highlighted exactly what I've been saying - if we get lazy on the hard yards, we're a very vulnerable team.

"We have to be, as I've been consistent all along, at our absolute best to get results.

"I've sensed a little bit of subconscious complacency and my job is to ensure that doesn't seep into their performance."

Pressley on wanting to 'crawl under a rock', complacency & 'direct' culture

Hearts bounce back from 'rocky patch' with Dens 'demolition'

Pressley believes "there is a little bit of fragility in the squad - certain players of huge talent but a little bit fragile mentally" and must now lift them to face a Hibernian side on Tuesday who are hurting from a 4-0 home defeat by Dundee United.

"It's been a difficult 24, 48 hours," he admitted. "There's been a lot of hurt, a lot of embarrassment.

"At times, I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide on the back of such a disappointing result.

"But I will say this, you know I suffer a lot from vulnerability at times, but for some reason during difficult moments, I seem to find strength from somewhere. I do and I've had to show strength.

"But we had a good meeting on Sunday. We chatted a lot about the various aspects and hopefully we can start responding to the disappointment."

Pressley said he knew pre-match "that we're nowhere near as good as people tell us we are" and he had previously tried "various things" to guard against a poor performance.

"I've been trying to introduce a couple of things within their training, within our debriefs on games," he revealed.

"But obviously what I have tried to do hasn't had the right effect and, when you get a performance like Saturday, which lacked that intensity, lacked those hard yards, that's on me because I have to make sure that they're ready for that."

It was the first time the former Scotland centre-half has suffered such a heavy defeat as a player or manager.

"There's been some really disappointing days, disappointing results, but of course when you're the head coach and it's my responsibility then this ranks as one of the worst," he added.

"I've been in football for nearly 36 years and you think what have I not experienced and then this comes along. It's the great thing about football - it just keeps testing you.

"We have to use days like this as a reminder to ourselves - as a reset moment. I just hope we can bring some pride back to the football club with the right type of performance against Hibs."

#742. Who Is Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Wife Lori Huang?

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to stepping outside his marriage with a woman believed to be a foreign spy. Meet the woman caught in the middle.

Currently loading: all the data on Jensen Huang’s wife Lori Huang.

The Nvidia CEO made headlines earlier this month after he admitted to having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a woman the US government suspects to be a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. And while his actions may have posed a threat to national security, it was the breach in Jensen’s personal life that he expressed the most regret over.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he wrote in a Nov. 8 statement. “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty.”

“Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together,” he added. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

And though Jensen resigned from his position, less than two weeks later the tech company’s board ultimately decided to reboot his position as President and Chief Executive Officer while an investigation into the matter continues.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” he said in a Nov. 23 statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

But “above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family.”

Keep reading for a closer look into all the information uploaded about the matriarch of that family.

Sparks flew when Jensen, 63, and Lori, 64, were paired up as lab partners during electrical engineering class while attending Oregon State University in the early 1980s.

“There were, like, 250 kids in electrical engineering, and maybe three girls,” he told The New Yorker in 2023. “I tried to impress her—not with my looks, of course, but with my strong capability to complete homework.”

And it was over doing homework together than Jensen finally gained the courage to ask her out on a date, a piece of their love story he shared he’d never forget.

As he put it in a 2022 press release, “That was the most important, single event of OSU, and of my life.”

In 1985, the couple tied the knot, eight years before Jensen co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsk and Curtis Priem in 1993.

Though Jensen certainly put in the work to get where he is today, he previously credited his marriage to his wife (born Lori Mills) for the success of his multi-trillion-dollar tech company.

“It’s good to have someone in your life who unconditionally believes in you, who believes you’re doing your best,” he told the Oregon State College of Engineering publication in 2014. “You need people like that, and Lori’s always been that person for me—ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it.”

He continued, “Even when I had self-doubts, she didn’t.”

After the Huang family—and Nvidia—was shaken by Jensen’s affair, he reiterated his commitment to his and Lori’s decades-long marriage.

“To my wife and family: I love you,” he said in a Nov. 8 statement. “I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.”

Jensen and Lori share daughter Madison, 35, as well as son Spencer, 36, together—and they’re both in on the family business.

Madison earned her MBA from London Business School and joined her dad’s company in 2020, where she currently works as Nvidia’s senior director of product and technical marketing, according to her company bio.

Meanwhile, Spencer earned his MBA from New York University and joined Nvidia in 2022, where he works as the company’s director of product management for robotics, according to his LinkedIn.

Lori is president of her and Jensen’s Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, the couple’s private charitable foundation, according to IRS filings cited by CNBC.

Established in 2007, the company was estimated to have $9.2 billion in assets in June 2025, per the outlet, and even gave a $50 million grant to build the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Collaborative Innovation Complex at their alma mater back in 2022.

In a press release about the sizable donation, Jensen and Lori emphasized the critical role OSU played in their early careers as microchip designers in Silicon Valley after graduation.

“We discovered our love for computer science and engineering at OSU,” they said in a joint statement. “We hope this gift will help inspire future generations of students also to fall in love with technology and its capacity to change the world.”

#741. Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case

Sadio Mane was named best player at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations

Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.

Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.

On Tuesday afternoon sport's highest legal authority, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), will render its judgement on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they won in January against the hosts in Rabat.

The case was heard in early October, and the wait is almost over.

With 66,000 fans creating an electric atmosphere in the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco were chasing their first Afcon title since 1976.

But the final descended into chaos deep into second-half stoppage time.

With the match goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had blown for a Morocco free-kick.

The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a video assistant referee (VAR) review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.

Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.

Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.

The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing that Senegal had breached competition regulations.

Article 82, contained within a chapter titled 'Withdrawals', states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team... refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee", they shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated from the current competition".

In March a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.

While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, some people, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.

The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.

Some Senegal supporters were initially convicted of hooliganism offences after clashes during the final but eventually returned home after receiving a royal pardon

Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.

For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.

More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.

The FSF's appeal was heard in private on 8 October by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.

The panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based attorney and professor of âlaw at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas completed the trio.

If the panel had failed to come to a consensus on the case, Cas president Simon will have made the final decision.

Although Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.

Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in March that it will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so, if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.

The Senegal walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at â a âreferee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.

"This new rule will also apply âto any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match âto be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."

Thiaw lost his job following Senegal's last-32 World Cup exit this summer, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Morocco dugout in January, was dismissed in March.

Whatever the outcome of the case, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.

The FMRF's senior hierarchy was furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.

The FSF and the Senegalese government have leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.

Other incidents also irked Senegal, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.

With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.

While the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

#740. Boxing Champ Tyson Fury Shares Schizophrenia Diagnosis

Boxer Tyson Fury shared he was diagnosed with schizophrenia after becoming the heavyweight champion of the world in 2015: “Words can’t explain the darkness I was in.”

Tyson Fury is detailing a decadelong personal battle.

The boxing champ shared in his upcoming Netflix documentary that he was diagnosed with schizophrenia back in 2015, the same year he became the heavyweight champion of the world following his victory over Wladimir Klitschko.

“Words can’t explain the darkness I was in,” Tyson says in the self-titled doc, out Nov. 27, according to Deadline. “I came from the living version of the pits of hellfire. And I 100 percent thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.”

Two years later, he got even more insight into the war raging inside his mind.

“I was waking up in the night like this, the anxiety was crippling me. I just could not overcome it,” he explains. “Completely gone, and that’s when I went and saw the psychiatrist down in London. She asked me like a gazillion questions, and I ticked all the boxes, whatever was going on. Depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder.”

And while the 38-year-old only just began addressing his mental health struggles in recent years, his father John Fury shares in the doc that he saw signs of the athlete’s diagnoses all along.

“I can tell you this: When I look back, it’s always been there,” the patriarch admits. “Me being who I am and no understanding of anything, I didn’t want to see a depressed kid—and if I did see it, I paid no mind to it.”

That’s because if he did, he’d have to face his own mental health struggles. “But I understand now,” John adds. “It’s an illness, a terrible illness. I suffer with it myself.”

But on Halloween 2017, Tyson—who shares seven kids with wife Paris Fury—decided he would make a change.

“I went out and I was embarrassed of how I looked,” he recalls. “I had this big costume on, a glow in the dark skeleton suit and I thought no one would recognize me in this.”

But instead of focusing on keeping a low profile, he couldn’t help but take a hard look at his life.

“I looked around me and I could see all like young people and I thought I’ve had the world in my hands and I threw it all away,” he notes. “And now, I’m just a fat mess, addicted to alcohol and, go home.”

But it was hitting rock bottom that allowed him to eventually reach the pinnacle of his life.

“I just said, ‘I can’t do this on my own anymore. I need your help,’” he says in the doc. “And that was the part, the comeback.”

Keep reading for more stars who have spoken out about their mental health struggles…

The Grammy winner has been very open about how she protects her energy, such as ignoring haters on social media, while also sharing her advice for those who may need help.

"When people ask me what I'd say to somebody looking for advice on mental health, the only thing I can say is patience," she told Vogue. "I had patience with myself. I didn't take that last step. I waited. Things fade."

The Frozen star has talked for years about her strategies for coping with her mental health at public keynotes and even on her Instagram Stories.

She has advocated for finding the methods that help you best, which for her, according to Health, can include medication, listing ten positive things in her life for every negative thought and getting plenty of exercise.

While everyone was trying to make the best of socially distancing to slow the coronavirus pandemic, the "Firework" artist got real about how situations like this can also be extremely stressful.

"Sometimes I don't know what's worse trying to avoid the virus or the waves of depression that come with this new norm," she shared on Twitter. Katy talked about how she manages those waves, writing, "There is not really anywhere to go besides my car. So I go to my car a lot. That is my safe space."

The model, who teamed up with designer Kenneth Cole to raise awareness for The Mental Health Coalition, spoke on Good Morning America about her own experiences with anxiety.

She recalled after her panic attacks started recurring, she, "finally kind of got the information that I needed about it."

"For me, I have good days and I have some really anxious days, so I'm really off and on," Kendall expressed, adding that was why she wanted to become involved with the movement. "What I hope to accomplish is for people to not feel as alone."

The rapper (real name Radric Davis) revealed in his October 2025 book Episodes: The Diary of a Recovering Mad Man that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which prompted a mental health episode in 2020.

“After that, I was like, ‘Man, I got to really just hold myself accountable and take care of my health,’” he said on an episode of The Breakfast Club. “I don’t never want to have an episode again. I’m gonna see a therapist, [even] if I have to take medicine.”

In addition to his hope that his vulnerability would help others in need, Gucci Mane said that his kids Ice Davis and Iceland Ka’oir Davis with wife Keyshia Ka’Oir inspired him to seek help amid his episode.

“My wife was pregnant with my little boy,” he continued. “I don’t want to raise a family and then my mental health [is] gone. What if I have an episode I can’t come back from? So, I just started doing the work and started seeking help.”

In October 2026, the daughter of Teresa Giudice and Joe Giudice shared she was getting treatment for bipolar disorder in a candid update about her mental health journey.

"I do struggle with mental health issues," Milania told followers in an Oct. 12 Instagram video. "I am bipolar. I struggle with depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD and I am not ashamed of any of my mental health disorders because I'm currently at a treatment center, my mom's on her way to come visit me today."

The then-20-year-old added that "this summer hit me like a bus" after Milania was arrested for assault in May and her best friend Victoria Zardoya died suddenly in July.

"A lot of things happened in a short amount of time and I'm trying to just process everything," the University of Tampa student noted. "It's really hard being in the public light while you go through things in life."

The Gossip Girl alum detailed his experience as a child actor with what he described as "body dysmorphia."

“I know that I hated my body,” Penn told The Guardian in April 2025, “and simply wanted a different one.”

In response to the weight he gained following his parents' divorce, he added,  “There was just a period where, coming out of depression and isolation, I was jumping wilfully into, but also being thrust into, this world where the more conventionally beautiful I seemed, the more successful I might be, the more value I might have.”

Despite the mental struggles, though, Penn credited his ability to persist to his spirituality.

“That is what allowed me to persevere through the disillusionment, all the things I’d been grappling with,” he explained, “and then come back to it all, but with hopefully some kind of inner transformation.”

The Scrubs alum has been vocal about her past difficult relationship with food.

“Some may call it an eating disorder, I just call it my life,” she said on the The Funny Thing Is podcast. “My drug of choice was always food. I did crazy s--t with it.”

She added, “I would over-exercise, and there was a sprinkle of bulimia in there.”

Though she has confessed her struggles with her diet, she has also shared her progress with her health and fitness goals.

“When I was 23, I cut all sugar out of my diet, quit drinking, and found yoga and breathing and stretching,” she told Bon Appétit in 2017. “That’s the best Ritalin you could give anyone."

She continued, "I’m an actress with food issues and body image issues—that's real. But I'm trying to heal that part of myself and also handle my physical issues naturally by putting the best things into my body."

The Full House alum reflected on her mental health journey and navigating her battle with depression.

"It's very difficult to speak out about it, even to your most trusted people," she shared on her Candace Cameron Bure Podcast. "At least for me, I feel like I should be strong enough to overcome that and then it feels so weak."

The Black Adam actor has been open about having depression and how it can be difficult for men to talk about their mental health.

"We all go thru the sludge/shit and depression never discriminates. Took me a long time to realize it but the key is to not be afraid to open up," he wrote on Twitter. "Especially us dudes have a tendency to keep it in. You're not alone."

The Duke of Sussex helped break down some of the stigma around seeking help for mental health when, in an interview with the Telegraph, he opened up about his own journey with therapy. As he told the outlet, "The experience I have had is that once you start talking about it, you realize that actually you're part of quite a big club."

Another proponent of seeking professional help, the Empire star has been open about her struggles with depression."I have a therapist that I speak to," she previously told Variety. "That's the only way I can get through it."

Taraji even started The Boris Lawrence Henson Foundation, which works to reduce the stigma around mental health in the African American community and also works to increase the number of Black therapists.

The Grammy winner explained that experiences with an eating disorder and stage freight led her to start a form of PTSD treatment called MDMA and and psilocybin therapy.

“I was touring without stage fright for the first time,” she told Rolling Stone in May 2025. “There was a hook around my guts and everyone in the room was having the same feeling, [like] there’d been a huge pressure change. It made me realize how much I love and kind of need that very deep, visceral response to feel my music.”

She added that her renewed focus on her mental health, as well as her decision to stop taking birth control, caused her understanding of her own gender to become “more expansive.”

“I felt like stopping taking my birth control, I had cut some sort of cord between myself and this regulated femininity,” she continued. “It sounds crazy, but I felt that all of a sudden, I was off the map of femininity. And I totally believed that that allowed things to open up.”

"When I was in middle school, I was struggling with severe anxiety and depression and the help and support I received from my family and a therapist saved my life," the Riverdale actress wrote on Instagram in 2017.  "Asking for help is the first step. You are more precious to this world than you'll ever know."

The “What He Didn’t Do” singer shared insight into what her life has been like during her yearslong battle with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

“I would have told you three years ago my anxiety started during my divorce in Covid,” Carly said an August 2025 episode of Bunnie Xo’s Dumb Blonde podcast. “But I’ve had crippling OCD since I was a child.”

“I got really conditioned over the last 10 years to just zip it up and deal with it, and it just kind of got to a place where a couple years ago I just had to really start back into therapy, start really, like, trying to figure out all of these different things,” she continued. “Like, recognizing OCD was something—no, that didn’t come in 2020, that’s been there since I was 6 or 7.”

While the cookbook author is the proud parent to four kiddos, she's also been open about postpartum depression that many new mothers experience but feel like they cannot talk about.

"It got easier and easier to say it aloud every time," she wrote in an open letter to Glamour in 2017. "I want people to know it can happen to anybody and I don't want people who have it to feel embarrassed or to feel alone."

While promoting her book Mirror, Mirror, the model opened up to The Edit magazine about facing depression and suicidal thoughts as a teenager, saying she felt "something dark" in her during that time.

"I relied too much on love, too much on other people to make me happy, and I needed to learn to be happy by myself," Cara told the publication, via W. "So now I can be by myself, I can be happy. It took me a long time."

The "Thank U, Next" artist has encouraged fans to seek help if they need, responding to a Twitter user who joked about wondering who Ariana's therapist is with, "lmaoaoo this is funny as f--k but in all honesty therapy has saved my life so many times."

"If you're afraid to ask for help, don't be," she continued. "u don't have to be in constant pain & u can process trauma. I've got a lot of work to do but it's a start to even be aware that it's possible."

The singer has been open about her journey with addiction, sobriety, mental health and more, including many of those aspects of her life within her music.

She also continually reminds fans that working on your mental health is an ongoing process where there will be some bad days, previously writing on Instagram, "A reminder to anyone struggling out there - this life is a journey with tons of ups and downs but you can't give up."

Not only has the actress taken on roles that deal with mental health, such as her role as Rue in the teen drama Euphoria, she's also addressed those issues in her own life, too.

Back in 2013, Zendaya wrote on her now-defunct app that she struggled with anxiety after an appearance on Ellen where her mic went out. She has since learned ways to manage those feelings, adding, "Sometimes you just have to take a step back so things stop stressin' you."

The singer candidly described her mental health journey with WSJ Magazine, saying, "My highs were really high, and my lows would take me out for weeks at a time."

"I found out I do suffer from mental health issues," she shared. "I got on the right medication, and my life has been completely changed."

The Grammy winner made it her mission to spread kindness and be open about mental health, including her own.

"I have struggled for a long time, both being public and not public about my mental health issues or my mental illness," she said during the Global Changemakers Award at Children Mending Hearts' Empathy Rocks fundraiser in 2018. "But, I truly believe that secrets keep you sick."

#739. Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

#738. When is the Euro 2028 qualifying draw?

The home nations have been allocated their pots for Euro 2028 qualifying

The Euro 2028 qualifying draw will take place on Sunday, 6 December at 17:00 GMT at the International Convention Centre in Belfast.

It will form the twelve groups that make up the qualifying group stage; six containing four teams and six containing five teams.

All 54 Uefa member associations will enter qualifying at the group stage.

Despite hosting the 2028 tournament, the UK home nations and the Republic of Ireland must also participate in qualifying rounds.

England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland will host the Euro 2028 tournament

The 54 teams have been divided into five pots based on their interim overall ranking in the 2026-27 Nations League following the conclusion of the league phase.

Pots one to four contain 12 teams, and pot five contains six teams.

The teams will then be drawn into the 12 qualifying groups, with the four host teams, as well as Northern Ireland, drawn into different groups.

The four winners of the Nations League quarter-finals must be drawn into a group containing four teams.

Twenty teams, made up of 12 group winners and eight best runners-up, will advance directly to the tournament proper. The eight highest-ranking runners-up will be based on the overall qualifying rankings.

If host nations fail to win or are runners-up in their group, there will be two spaces in the tournament proper reserved for the best-ranked nations at the end of the group stage, regardless of how many other host nation teams have qualified.

As a result, the final number of teams in the tournament proper will be between 20 and 22 nations, depending on the performance of the host nations.

There are also qualifying routes available through the 2026-27 Nations League.

Nations League final rankings will also determine the seeding of nations for Euro 2028 qualification.

You can read more on how the process works here.

Pot One: England, Portugal, France, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Netherlands, Norway, Greece, Italy, Denmark, Croatia

Pot Two: Wales, Serbia, Turkey, Czech Republic, Switzerland, Sweden, Austria, Northern Ireland, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hungary, Republic of Ireland

Pot Three: Ukraine, Scotland, Kosovo, Poland, Israel, Romania, Georgia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Iceland, Slovakia

Pot Four: Estonia, Belarus, Faroe Islands, Cyprus, Finland, Moldova, Armenia, Bulgaria, Kazakhstan, Luxembourg, Latvia, San Marino

Pot Five: Malta, Azerbaijan, Lithuania, Andorra, Gibraltar, Liechtenstein

Matchday seven: 30 September-2 October 2027

Wembley Stadium will host two of England's group-stage matches should they qualify for the final tournament

If the host nations and/or Northern Ireland qualify for the tournament proper, they will have dedicated slots at stadiums:

England (Group B): Etihad Stadium (one match), Wembley Stadium (two matches)

Northern Ireland (Group D): Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (one match), Villa Park (one match), Wembley Stadium (one match)

Republic of Ireland (Group E): Dublin Arena (three matches)

Scotland (Group F): Hampden Park (three matches)

Wales (Group A): National Stadium of Wales (three matches)

If the hosts and/or Northern Ireland qualify via the play-offs, they will still be assigned to their designated group, but will not play all their group matches in the locations mentioned above.

#737. Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany

His life is a reflection of contemporary German history, addressed via his songs and sharp wit. At 90, he's as feisty as ever.

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama."

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism."

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer."

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. "

I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.

He became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom."

The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

This article was originally written in German.

The former Grey's Anatomy star sparked a feud with the series creator in 2008 when she removed her name from the Emmy Awards consideration. Heigl stated that her reason for the move was because she wasn't "given the material to warrant a nomination."

Rhimes later opened up about Heigl's decision during an interview with Oprah Winfrey on Oprah's Next Chapter in 2012. "On some level it stung and on some level I was not surprised," she said. "When people show you who they are, believe them. I carry that [mantra] with me a lot. It has served me well."

It was the New York Fashion Week fight heard 'round the world when Nicki and Cardi got into a heated altercation at the Harper's Bazaar Icon party. The following month, Cardi opened up about the catalyst for the fight with Nicki.

"For a while now she's been taking a lot of shots at me," Cardi said in W magazine's Art Issue. "I spoke to her twice before, and we came to an understanding. But she kept it going."

The real spark of the fight came when Cardi saw that Nicki had allegedly liked and then unliked a tweet about Cardi's parenting skills, which Nicki has denied.

"I was going to make millions off my Bruno Mars tour, and I sacrificed that to stay with my daughter," Cardi continued. "I love my daughter. I'm a good-ass f--king mom. So for somebody that don't have a child to like that comment? So many people want to say that party wasn't the time or the place, but I'm not going to catch another artist in the grocery store or down the block."

Tension between Kanye and Taylor first started in 2009, when the "Stronger" rapper took the stage during her acceptance speech at the MTV Video Music Awards. Years later, the two would make up and even become friends, but that came to an end in 2016 after the release of his song "Famous," in which he name-checks the "End Game" singer.

In February 2025, one day before the Grammys, Kanye updated his Instagram to follow only Taylor. He added no further comment, and his fellow musician did not respond publicly to the move.

Carey and J.Lo's supposed feud started when the Queen of Christmas was asked to give her opinion on several singers during a 2003 German TV interview. When asked her opinion on Lopez, she replied, "I don't know her."
